details:
**Arrow's impossibility theorem**
Kenneth Arrow's 1951 result that no ranked (ordinal) voting system with three or more options can turn individual preferences into a community-wide ranking while satisfying all of a set of fairness criteria: unrestricted domain, Pareto efficiency, independence of irrelevant alternatives (IIA), and non-dictatorship. It is the single most common clue for voting.

**Condorcet paradox**
Named for the Marquis de Condorcet, this is the situation in which majority preferences become cyclic, like rock, paper, scissors: a majority prefers A to B, another majority B to C, and another C to A, so majority rule produces no winner. A "Condorcet method" or "Condorcet criterion" picks the candidate who would beat every rival head-to-head, if one exists.

**Downs' paradox (paradox of voting)**
Anthony Downs's observation, from An Economic Theory of Democracy (1957), that a rational, self-interested person should not vote, because the chance of casting the deciding ballot is tiny compared with the cost of voting. Expressive and altruistic theories of voting were proposed as responses to it.

**First-past-the-post**
The plurality, "winner takes all" system in which the candidate with the most votes wins even without a majority. It is used in the UK, the US, and India, and it encourages "wasted" votes and tactical voting. Block voting is a plurality variant for electing several seats at once.

**Tactical voting and the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem**
Tactical (strategic) voting means voting against your true preference to get a better outcome, such as backing a likely winner instead of a favored long shot. The Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem shows that any ranked voting rule with three or more possible outcomes is either dictatorial, limited to two possible winners, or open to tactical voting.

**Borda count**
A ranked system devised by Jean-Charles de Borda in which candidates get points based on their position on each ballot, and the highest total wins. It is vulnerable to tactical voting and to "cloning" (adding similar candidates to split support). Michael Dummett, who also published proofs of the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem in his work on voting procedures, proposed a variant of it.

**Bradley effect**
The tendency of polls to overstate support for a Black candidate because some white voters tell pollsters they will vote for him and then do not. It is named for Los Angeles mayor Tom Bradley, who led in the polls but narrowly lost the 1982 California governor's race, and it is often explained by social desirability bias. Exit polls, surveys of people who have just voted, are part of this story.

**Get Out the Vote (Donald Green and Alan Gerber)**
A book by political scientists Donald Green and Alan Gerber that uses field experiments to test which methods increase voter turnout, such as door-to-door canvassing, phone calls, and direct mail.

**Ranked-choice (instant-runoff) voting**
A system in which voters rank candidates. If no one has a majority, the last-place candidate is eliminated and those ballots go to their next choice, repeating until someone wins. It is the standard contrast to first-past-the-post. Runoff elections are a related two-round version.

**Median voter theorem (Duncan Black)**
Duncan Black's 1948 result that when voters' preferences lie along a single dimension and are single-peaked, majority rule picks the option preferred by the median voter. Candidates therefore move toward the center.

**Expressive voting (Geoffrey Brennan and Loren Lomasky)**
Brennan and Lomasky's answer to Downs' paradox, distinguishing "instrumental" motives (changing the result) from "expressive" ones (voting to show support for a cause or identity, like cheering at a game). Since expressive benefits do not depend on being decisive, voting can be rational.

**Cardinal (score) voting**
Systems in which voters give each candidate an independent grade or score instead of a ranking, such as score voting and approval voting. Since they are not ranked systems, they are usually said to escape Arrow's impossibility theorem and the Condorcet cycle.

**Jason Brennan**
A philosopher who wrote The Ethics of Voting and Against Democracy. In Against Democracy he sorts citizens into "hobbits," "hooligans," and "vulcans" by how much they know and care about politics, and he argues for epistocracy, where political power depends on knowledge.

**Michigan model**
The theory of voting from The American Voter (1960) by Angus Campbell and colleagues at the University of Michigan. It uses a "funnel of causality" in which long-term factors such as social background and party identification narrow down to the final choice in the voting booth.

**May's theorem**
Kenneth May's proof that when there are only two options, simple majority rule is the only voting rule that is anonymous, neutral, and positively responsive. It explains why majority rule works well with two choices and breaks down with more.
